rules.description: The protective stop sits a fixed buffer beyond the extreme of the last N bars (for a long, the lowest low of the window ending one bar ago); the close breaking that level takes the trade off.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= lowest(low[1], rangeLookback) - stopBuffer

complexity.reason: a window extreme plus a fixed buffer

catalog_match.note: identical test, same window ending one bar ago, same buffer in points

rules.merge_notes: Four restatements of one window-extreme stop: 'Stop B' beyond the tested support (G04-08), the failure test's excursion extreme (G06-09), the Anti's pre-Anti trend extreme at lookback 50 (G06-37) and the higher-timeframe range (G10-08, this rule at a 5x lookback per decision 4; its min() picks the WIDER stop, so not an OR composite).

rules.description: The same window-extreme stop, but the buffer past the obvious level is scaled by ATR instead of fixed in points, so it widens with volatility.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= lowest(low[1], rangeLookback) - bufferAtrMultiple * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: a window extreme plus an ATR

catalog_match.note: add bufferAtrMultiple and atrLookback inputs; stopBuffer stays for the fixed-points form and the two are alternatives, not additive

rules.merge_notes: G06-25 (stray from pullbacks_continuation) is Grimes's own preference for this wider pattern-geometry stop over the tight trigger-bar stop, restating G06-17's formula verbatim. Grimes wants the buffer scaled, not fixed: 'a few ticks beyond the obvious levels' still gets swept in extra volatility. Both sources are the existing stop with an ATR-scaled buffer. G06-17's extra random jitter is not carried (non-deterministic). Grimes names no multiple; 0.25 ATR is the miner's default.

rules.description: The stop sits beyond the worst price the trade has seen since entry: for a long, the lowest low from the entry bar through the previous bar, minus an offset.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= 1 && close[0] <= lowest(low[1], ctx.BarsSinceEntry()) - ratchetOffset

complexity.reason: a running adverse extreme held since the fill bar

catalog_match.note: same running extreme, same one-bar-back window; the catalog rule already notes it only widens and is not a trail

rules.merge_notes: 'The ultimate stop is above the extreme of the initial pullback thrust' is the running adverse extreme from the entry bar to the previous bar, which is the catalog rule exactly. Buffer is in ticks in the source and in points in the catalog; same level.

rules.description: The running-extreme stop with its window reaching back before the fill, so it covers the whole base the position was accumulated in, not just the bars held.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= lowest(low[1], ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + preEntryBars) - stopOffsetTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: a window whose length grows with the holding period

catalog_match.note: one new input, preEntryBars; preEntryBars 0 is the existing rule

rules.merge_notes: 'Put a stop below the lowest point reached while the market was in the base.' The base predates the fill, so the window has to run back past it. baseLookback 10 is the miner's default, not a number Grimes gives.

rules.description: The stop sits at the low of the bar exactly N bars back (short: the high), a fixed-offset trail that needs no window scan.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= low[nBarsAgo]

complexity.reason: a bare fixed-offset comparison

catalog_match.note: that rule takes the extreme OF a window; this takes one specific bar's extreme, so the level is not monotone and can loosen as well as tighten

rules.merge_notes: 'Stop out at the lowest low of three days ago' is ambiguous. The single-bar reading is taken: it is the cheaper mechanization, and the window reading would simply duplicate StopBeyondRecentRangeExtreme. The authoring pass should note the level is not a true trail.

rules.description: The stop sits a tick or two beyond the signal/trigger bar's own extreme opposite the trade, and stays there.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= sigLow - stopOffsetTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: one captured bar extreme plus a tick offset

catalog_match.note: the candidate's triggerBarLag 0 is the signal bar the catalog rule already captures

rules.merge_notes: The tight-stop school for a lower-timeframe breakout trigger: a tick beyond the trigger bar. Grimes records it only to say he prefers the wider pattern stop (G06-17, merged as StopBeyondRangeExtremeAtrBuffer).

rules.description: The most recent confirmed swing extreme is captured on the fill bar and the stop sits a tick beyond it for the life of the trade.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && haveStopLong && close[0] <= stopLong - stopTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection, captured once at entry

catalog_match.note: same frozen-at-entry pivot level and tick offset

rules.merge_notes: G02-05 (stray from pullbacks_continuation) is the same stop stated as the trend-invalidation point: the pullback swing extreme that defined the entry, captured at entry, with its stopBuffer being this rule's stopTicks. The complex pullback's stop beyond the second (CD) leg's termination point is the most recent confirmed swing extreme at entry, which is the catalog rule. The leg identity comes from the entry rule, not the stop, so nothing new is needed here.

rules.description: The same frozen-at-entry swing stop, but placed beyond the Nth most recent confirmed pivot rather than the nearest one: a wider stop that is much less likely to be hit.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && haveStopLong && close[0] <= swingLow(pivotIndex, pivotStrength) - stopTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: a pivot scan that has to reach a rank deeper than the most recent confirmed pivot

catalog_match.note: add a pivotIndex input; pivotIndex 1 is the existing rule, and SwingPivotTarget already carries exactly this input with the scan to match

rules.merge_notes: 'It is possible to step back to the penultimate pivot, with the trade-off of a much smaller position size.' One new input on the existing stop. stopLookback has to widen with pivotIndex so the scan can reach the deeper pivot.

rules.description: On a failure test the stop is placed AT or just INSIDE the swing extreme being tested, rather than beyond it: a few extra premature stop-outs bought in exchange for much less slippage on the exits that matter.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && haveStopLong && close[0] <= swingLow(1, pivotStrength) + insideTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: the same pivot capture as InitialStopBeyondSwingAtEntry, with the offset on the other side of the level

catalog_match.note: allow stopTicks to take NEGATIVE values; the signed-offset convention already exists on SwingHighProfitTarget's offsetTicks

rules.merge_notes: Grimes deliberately inverts the usual convention on failure tests: stop inside the tested extreme, ahead of the crowd's stop cluster. Mechanically that is the existing stop with a negative offset, so this needs a signed input and a grid that goes below zero, not a new rule.

rules.description: The stop sits a fraction of the way from the entry price toward the tested range extreme, inside the zone rather than beyond it, so the exit happens before the mass of resting stops at the level.
rules.pseudocode: levelLow = lowest(low[1], levelLookback) captured on the fill bar; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice() - stopFraction * (ctx.EntryPrice() - levelLow)

complexity.reason: a window extreme captured at entry and a fraction-of-distance comparison

catalog_match.note: identical arithmetic, different far anchor: the tested range extreme here, the signal bar's low there

rules.merge_notes: Grimes's 'Stop A', inside the support level: it 'virtually eliminates slippage even in thin markets because you are exiting long before the mass of other stop orders is hit'. His fraction is measured from the entry, the catalog rule's from the level; the two are complementary.

rules.description: The initial stop sits a multiple of ATR from the entry price, the ATR captured once on the fill bar and the level then fixed for the life of the trade.
rules.pseudocode: riskPts = atrMult * atr(atrLength) captured on ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0; ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < -riskPts * ctx.BigPointValue()

complexity.reason: an ATR captured at entry and frozen

catalog_match.note: that rule's stop leg is this test, and its hook states the risk is captured ONCE on the fill bar and frozen; its take-profit leg is ORed in off the same risk unit

rules.merge_notes: 'It would be very unusual to set an initial stop less than two ATRs from price, and it may sometimes be more than four.' Book range 2 to 4 (catalog default 2), so this is a grid range, not a rule. Grimes allows ADR or a one-day standard deviation as the same family's volatility unit.

rules.description: A floor on initial stop distance: whatever the pattern says, the stop is never closer to the entry than the average range of one bar on the trading timeframe, because closer than that is inside the noise.
rules.pseudocode: stopDistance = max(patternStopDistance, atr(atrLength)); ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < -stopDistance * ctx.BigPointValue()

complexity.reason: an ATR and a max()

catalog_match.note: the floor turned into an actual stop is that rule at stopAtrMultiple 1

rules.merge_notes: Not a placement rule: it is a clamp on whichever stop rule is used, and ORed exits cannot clamp one another. Its real content is a grid constraint - no stop-distance input should be optimized below one average bar range. Raised as a design decision for the design-grid pass.

rules.description: LeBeau's chandelier: the stop hangs a fixed number of ATRs below the highest high made since entry (short: above the lowest low), with no acceleration factor.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= highest(high, ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + 1) - atrMult * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: a running peak since entry plus an ATR

catalog_match.note: MaxPositionProfit is the VERIFIED INTRABAR peak, so MaxPositionProfit - OpenPositionProfit equals (highest high since entry - close) x BigPointValue and the catalog test reduces to close < highestHighSinceEntry - multiple x ATR: the chandelier, bar entry-side costs

rules.merge_notes: The miner suspected the equivalence; the algebra above confirms it. AtrTrailingStop re-reads the ATR each bar, which is also LeBeau's original. Grimes offers it as 'the Parabolic without the acceleration factor', which is exactly how it pairs with ParabolicSarTrailingStop below.

rules.description: Wilder's Parabolic SAR used as an exit-only trailing stop: the stop starts from the trend's extreme point and is ratcheted toward price every bar by an acceleration factor that itself steps up each time a new extreme prints.

complexity.reason: a recursive, self-accelerating state variable plus an extreme-point tracker, both carried across every bar of the position

catalog_match.note: name overlap only: that rule compares two successive leg magnitudes to detect an unsustainable slope. No SAR recursion exists anywhere in the corpus

rules.merge_notes: The literal SAR recursion, carried once and exit-only (never stop-and-reverse). State resets on ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0, the corpus's per-position capture idiom. Wilder's standard 0.02/0.02/0.20 defaults; Grimes presents it as the archetype of an accelerating trail.

rules.description: Trail the stop under the Nth most recent confirmed swing low (short: above the Nth swing high), re-read every bar and checked on closes only: rank 1 is the tight trail, rank 2 the wider one.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && havePivot && close[0] <= swingLow(pivotIndex, pivotStrength) - trailOffsetTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection re-read every bar, at a rank deeper than the most recent pivot

catalog_match.note: add a pivotIndex input; pivotIndex 1 is the existing rule, which is already close-only as Grimes wants, and SwingPivotTarget carries the same input with the scan to copy

rules.merge_notes: 'In an uptrend a tight stop could be trailed under the highest pivot low of the trend; slightly wider stops could go under the second-highest, probably working both on a close-only basis.' The highest pivot low of an uptrend is the most recent one, so rank is the only new degree of freedom.

rules.description: A one-bar trail: the long is closed when the close falls to or below the previous bar's low, less a tick offset.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= low[1] - stopOffsetTicks * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: a bare comparison against the prior bar's extreme

catalog_match.note: at armProfitDollars 0 that rule is this one: arming is ctx.MaxPositionProfit(), which starts at 0 per position, so the trail is live from the fill bar

rules.merge_notes: 'A trader holding a long in a runaway trend could have worked a stop each day below the previous day's lows.' Grimes scopes it to a parabolic run; ungated it is a very aggressive universal trail. Supply the context as a separate filter placement, not as a change to the rule.

rules.description: The prior-bar trail with an ATR-scaled offset instead of a tick offset, so the day's allowed adverse move scales with volatility.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= low[1] - stopOffsetAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: a fixed-offset comparison plus an ATR window

catalog_match.note: add stopOffsetAtr and atrLength; the existing offset is in ticks and does not scale, and armProfitDollars 0 gives the unarmed form

rules.merge_notes: 'Consider stops that limit your loss on any one day, perhaps a certain ATR multiple from the previous day's high, low, or closing values.' The adverse extreme (low for a long) is taken as the anchor, matching the existing rule; the high and close anchors are recorded here rather than given an input.

rules.description: The long is closed after N consecutive closes each lower than the one before (short: N consecutive higher closes); N of 1 is the first-opposite-close stop.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && for i in 0..consecutiveBars-1: close[i] < close[i+1]

complexity.reason: a short loop of close-to-close comparisons

catalog_match.note: that rule counts FAVOURABLE closes (Davey's profit-take: a long exits after N RISING closes); this counts adverse ones. Same loop, opposite comparison, and no placement of the existing rule produces it. AdverseBodyCountExit is close-versus-open, a different test

rules.merge_notes: Grimes lists the first down close and two consecutive down closes as one menu of simple trailing stops; they are this test at consecutiveBars 1 and 2, so they merge. He flags the family as statistically naive (three down closes is usually primed for a bounce) - worth keeping, worth the warning.

rules.description: Once peak profit has reached a multiple of the initial risk, the stop moves to the entry price (or just inside it) for the rest of the trade.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.MaxPositionProfit() >= riskMultiple * stopDistance * ctx.BigPointValue() && close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice() - breakevenBuffer

complexity.reason: arms on the peak-profit accessor, then holds a fixed level

catalog_match.note: activationProfit is in dollars and riskMultiple x stopDistance x BigPointValue is a dollar figure, so the existing inputs already express both book cases; breakevenBuffer carries 'just under your entry point'

rules.merge_notes: Two statements of one rule at different arming levels: tighten to just under the entry at 1R (G08-07), move to exact breakeven at 2R once the first target is filled (G08-08). Both are BreakevenStop; only the activation number changes, which is a grid range.

rules.description: The breakeven stop is armed structurally: once N consecutive closes since entry have each moved in the trade's favour, a later close back at the entry price takes the trade off.
rules.pseudocode:
// armed latches once favorableRun >= favorableCloses since ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0
ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && armedLong && close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice()

complexity.reason: a per-position counter and a latched flag, both reset on the fill bar

catalog_match.note: identical shape and identical latch idiom; the arming condition differs - a run of favourable closes here, a run of closes holding on the EMA's correct side there

rules.merge_notes: 'Once a trade is working, once the market is moving in the intended direction, tighten stops to reduce open risk.' The counter and flag reset on ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0, exactly as in BreakevenStopAfterEmaHoldingRun. Grimes's worked example arms on 2 closes; he gives no general number.

rules.description: A time stop: if the trade has been open N bars and open profit is still at or below a threshold, leave at market instead of waiting for the stop.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= maxBars && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() <= profitThreshold

complexity.reason: a bar counter and a profit comparison, both accessors

catalog_match.note: add a profitThreshold input; at 0 the only difference from the existing rule is that exactly-zero profit fires here too

rules.merge_notes: Grimes's general time stop ('if a trade does not hit some predetermined profit limit within a certain time, exit') and the failure test's 'you should not have to wait more than three or four bars for the profit target' are the same rule: G10-04 is maxBars 4 with profitThreshold = riskMultiple x stopDistance x BigPointValue.

rules.description: Scratch a trade that never went anywhere: N bars after entry, peak profit has still not reached a fraction of one ATR, so the market has found equilibrium and the edge is gone.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= maxFlatBars && ctx.MaxPositionProfit() < flatThreshold * atr(atrLength) * ctx.BigPointValue()

complexity.reason: a bar counter, the peak-profit accessor and an ATR

catalog_match.note: the gate is PEAK profit scaled by ATR, not open profit in dollars: a trade that never got anywhere, rather than one that happens to be losing at this close

rules.merge_notes: 'The market may simply go flat after the trade is entered - strong evidence the edge is gone.' MaxPositionProfit (the VERIFIED intrabar peak) is the cheap measure of 'never moved'; the source's symmetric excursion would also need a running minimum. maxFlatBars 6 is the miner's guess. Arrived from exits_targets.

rules.description: Instead of a hard exit when the time stop expires, the allowed give-back shrinks toward zero as bars elapse since entry, so open risk decays continuously through the window.

complexity.reason: Grimes gives only an analogy to the Parabolic, no tightening curve; linear, accelerating and stepped all fit the text

catalog_match.note: same intention - a stop that tightens on its own schedule - but driven by elapsed bars rather than by new extremes; no catalog rule decays a stop on time

rules.merge_notes: 'Tighten the stop very close to current prices, moving it closer as time goes on, in a similar fashion to the Parabolic SAR.' The curve is the whole rule and the book does not give it. ParabolicSarTrailingStop already supplies the accelerating form he points at, which may make this redundant.

rules.description: The session gapped against the position and the market then broke out of the opening range the wrong way: dump the position immediately rather than waiting for the original stop.
rules.pseudocode:
// intraday; gapDown and orLow are session state fixed in the session's first openingBars bars
ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && gapDown && barsSinceSessionOpen > openingBars && low[0] < orLow

complexity.reason: session-boundary state: the gap sign at the first bar plus the opening range's extremes, carried in locals

catalog_match.note: the corpus's opening-range exits are targets (OpeningRangeMeasuredMoveTarget, SessionMidpointTarget); none reads the session's gap direction against an open position

rules.merge_notes: 'If the market opens down and immediately presses lower, or breaks lower out of an opening range, there is a good chance it could trend down all day. Long positions should be dumped immediately.' Session state is held in locals as in SessionMidpointTarget. Its companion G08-22 (widen the stop instead) is dropped.

rules.description: A confirmation-counted stop: the trade is closed once N consecutive closes have printed beyond the setup's own level (the base's support for a long), rather than on the first break of it.
rules.pseudocode:
// levelLow = lowest(low[1], levelLookback) captured on the fill bar
ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && for i in 0..confirmBars-1: close[i] < levelLow

complexity.reason: a captured level plus a short run count

catalog_match.note: add a confirmBars input - a run of closes beyond the level instead of one; ConsecutiveClosesBeyondEmaRun is the same shape with the EMA as the level

rules.merge_notes: 'Once the market consolidated below that support level the probabilities favoured a breakdown, so there was no sense riding the trade to the initial stop.' A consolidation beyond the level, not a poke through it. Grimes gives no count; 3 chosen. Arrived from exits_targets.

rules.description: Within the first few bars of entry, one strong bar against the trade scratches it for a small win or loss instead of holding for the original stop.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.BarsSinceEntry() <= scratchWindow && close[0] < open[0] && open[0] - close[0] >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: a bar-anatomy test plus a bars-since-entry gate

catalog_match.note: add a scratchWindow (BarsSinceEntry) gate, which turns a trail into a scratch; ExitOnWeakFollowThrough already carries exactly this kind of maxBarsAfterSpike input

rules.merge_notes: 'Developing price action may suggest the trend is losing integrity - scratch the trade.' Research as stated; mechanized as the catalog's opposite-strong-bar exit restricted to the first bars after entry. Grimes gives no bar count. Arrived from exits_targets.

rules.description: Flat, the most recently closed position lost, and the exit was only a bar or two ago: permission to take the same setup again after a stop-out on a fakeout.
rules.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() == 0 && ctx.BarsSinceExit() <= reentryBars && PositionProfit(1) < 0

complexity.reason: trade-history accessors only

catalog_match.note: same three accessor tests; the catalog rule additionally requires the losing trade to have been short-lived

rules.merge_notes: 'If you are stopped out on a fakeout it is necessary to rebuy with a new stop beyond the new extreme.' The candidate's extra close > low[1] reversal test is an independent entry condition (entries AND) already carried as DipBelowPriorLowCloseBackAbove / StopRunReclaimReentry; the 'new stop' is StopBeyondRecentRangeExtreme applied again.

dropped.reason: stray from pullbacks_continuation. Composition of BreakevenStopAtRiskMultiple + the measured-move zone being reached and then held (LegOneEqualsLegTwoTarget in exits_targets); ORed exit placements cannot arm or condition one another, and the engine has no accessor for 'the target zone was touched and not exceeded'

stray from pullbacks_continuation. Re-entry to full size after a partial exit: decision 24 settles that partial profit taking is not expressible (each tranche is a full placement), so the partialProfitTaken state this depends on does not exist in the single-net-position model; the bare pullback-to-entry-price test is BreakevenStop's level read from the entry side, not a new rule
composition of ReenterAfterQuickStopOut + the FailureTest entry rule; entries are ANDed, so the 'second failure test' needs no rule of its own
not mechanizable: it instructs WIDENING an existing stop (replace it with one under the session low) after a gap-down recovery, and ORed exits cannot cancel or loosen another placement's stop

options: add a min-distance clamp input to every stop rule
treat it as a grid floor: no stop-distance input optimized below one average bar range
design_decisions.recommended: grid floor, enforced by the design-grid pass - ORed exits cannot clamp one another, so a per-rule input would have to be added 20 times

options: linear decay of the allowed give-back over maxBars
stepped tightening at fixed bar counts
design_decisions.recommended: do not author a separate curve: place ParabolicSarTrailingStop, which is the accelerating form Grimes explicitly analogizes to, and keep the time stop as the hard NumBarsIfBelowProfitThreshold exit

bucket_summary: 33 candidates plus four strays from pullbacks_continuation collapsed to 27 rules plus 4 drops (the reconciliation pass merged G02-05 into InitialStopBeyondSwingAtEntry and G06-25 into StopBeyondRangeExtremeAtrBuffer, and dropped G06-39 and G08-28): initial stop placement (beyond a window extreme, beyond a swing pivot, an ATR multiple, inside the tested level), the whole trailing family (swing pivot, chandelier, literal Parabolic SAR, prior-bar, N-bars-ago, consecutive adverse closes), breakeven and tighten triggers, time stops and gap management. Ten are duplicates of the Brooks-derived exit family, which already covers window-extreme stops, swing stops, chandelier ATR trails, breakeven arming and prior-bar trails; the strongest single finding is that AtrTrailingStop IS the chandelier stop (MaxPositionProfit is the intrabar peak, so its test reduces to close < highest high since entry - multiple x ATR). The A-list is mostly one new input on an existing rule: pivotIndex on the two swing stops, a negative (signed) stopTicks for Grimes's stop-inside-the-level convention, an ATR-scaled buffer on two stops, a profitThreshold on NumBarsIfLosing, a confirmBars run and a BarsSinceEntry scratch gate. The only genuinely new machinery is the Parabolic SAR recursion (B). RISK MULTIPLES: the engine has no initial-risk accessor, so every 'exit at NR' here is expressed with a stopDistance parameter in points that the placement must be set to match whatever stop rule is paired with it - said once here rather than on each rule.
